title: Aida 14 vs 16 vs 18: Which Cross Stitch Fabric Should You Choose?

seo.title: Aida 14 vs 16 vs 18: Which Cross Stitch Fabric to Use
seo.meta_description: Compare 14, 16 and 18 count Aida for finished size, visibility, coverage and comfort so you can choose the right fabric for your cross stitch pattern.
seo.search_intent: Compare Aida fabric counts and choose the best one for a specific cross stitch project.

excerpt: Aida count changes the size and texture of your stitching, not its quality. Here is how to choose comfortably between 14, 16 and 18 count.
content_html:
When you first shop for cross stitch fabric, the numbers can feel oddly important: Aida 11, 14, 16, 18 and beyond. It is easy to assume that a higher number means a “better” fabric. It does not. The number simply tells you how many squares fit into one inch of fabric, which determines the size of each cross and the physical size of the finished design.

There is no universal winner between 14, 16 and 18 count Aida. All three can produce beautiful work. The useful choice depends on how much detail you want, how large you want the finished piece to be and how comfortable you are seeing and stitching through smaller holes.

What 14, 16 and 18 count actually mean

Fabric count tells you how many stitches fit in one inch. Fourteen-count Aida has 14 squares per inch, 16-count has 16 and 18-count has 18. As the count goes up, the squares become smaller. The chart itself does not change: a 100 × 100 stitch pattern still contains 100 × 100 stitches. Only its physical footprint changes.

Take a design that is 140 stitches wide. On 14-count Aida it measures 10 inches across. On 16-count it measures 8.75 inches, and on 18-count it is roughly 7.8 inches. That difference may determine whether the finished piece fits a particular frame or works in the space where you plan to display it.

The calculation is straightforward: divide the stitch count by the fabric count to get inches. If you work in centimeters, multiply the result by 2.54. Do this before cutting your fabric and remember to add extra fabric around all sides. That border is not stitched, but it gives you room to hold the work and options when you frame it.

Count also changes the visual density of the piece. On 14-count Aida, the crosses are larger and can give the finished work a more graphic, visibly stitched texture. On 18-count, the surface appears finer and more compact. For pixel-inspired or pop art designs, either effect can be attractive: you may want the individual crosses to be part of the look, or prefer the image to read more smoothly from a distance.

14-count Aida: comfortable, flexible and beginner-friendly

Fourteen-count Aida is recommended to beginners for good reasons. The holes are easy to see and there is enough space to move the needle without straining your eyes. A huge number of commercial patterns also give their example measurements for 14 count, so it is easy to picture how large a project will become.

Two strands of cotton floss often give balanced coverage on 14 count, although the ideal amount depends on the fabric color, thread color and the look you prefer. Dark floss on pale fabric may leave tiny glimpses of cloth between the crosses. Some stitchers like that visible texture, while others use three strands for a fuller appearance.

Fourteen count is particularly good for decorative pieces that will be seen from a little distance: framed art, names, graphic motifs and lettering. Because the finished design is larger than it would be on higher counts, even a fairly compact pattern can have a satisfying presence on a wall.

The main drawback appears when you need a very small finished size or want an especially fine surface. A huge pattern on 14 count can require a lot of fabric. If a chart contains many thousands of stitches and you want the final piece to stay reasonably compact, moving to 16 or 18 count can be a practical choice.

16 and 18 count Aida: when a smaller grid makes sense

Sixteen-count Aida is an excellent middle ground. The holes are still comfortable for many stitchers, but the final piece is a little smaller and the surface looks slightly finer. If you have finished a project or two on 14 count and want to experiment with a more compact scale, 16 count is usually an easy transition.

Eighteen-count Aida produces an even finer finish. It is useful when a chart contains lots of detail, when you want to reduce the size of a large design or when you prefer the fabric grid to be less visually dominant. The trade-off is obvious: the holes are smaller, and long sessions can be more demanding on your eyes.

Lighting becomes increasingly important as the count rises. A bright, even lamp can completely change the experience, especially on dark fabric. Placing a light-colored cloth or surface behind dark Aida can also make the holes easier to identify.

Do not assume you must use exactly the same number of floss strands on every count. Two strands are common on 14 and 16 count. Many stitchers still use two on 18 for strong coverage, while others prefer one or two depending on the design. If the pattern gives a specific recommendation, start there and make a small test patch at the edge if you are unsure.

How to choose the right Aida for a specific pattern

Start with finished size. Calculate the chart dimensions on 14, 16 and 18 count, then compare them with the hoop, frame or wall space you have in mind. Next consider comfort. If this is your first project or small holes are difficult for you to see, 14 count will usually feel more relaxed. If you already stitch comfortably and want a finer result, 16 or 18 may suit you better.

Then look at the visual style. A design made from large blocks of bold color can look wonderful on 14 count because the crosses have real presence. A detailed portrait, landscape with many shades or very large chart may benefit from the finer appearance of 16 or 18. This is not an artistic rule; it is simply another way to control scale and texture.

Consider the fabric you already own too. You can usually change count without changing the chart as long as you continue to stitch one cross per square, but you must recalculate the finished dimensions and margins. Thread use can also change because the physical size is different and coverage depends on the number of strands.

If you are torn between two counts, stitch a tiny 10 × 10 square sample using one of the main colors. In a few minutes you can see whether you like the coverage, whether the holes are comfortable to see and whether the size of the crosses matches the look you want. That test tells you more than any universal recommendation.

For a first project, 14-count Aida is an easy choice. If you want to reduce the finished size without making the grid dramatically smaller, 16 count is beautifully balanced. If you prefer a fine result and enjoy working on a tighter grid, 18 count can look excellent. The best count is simply the one that gives the design the scale you want while keeping the hours of stitching comfortable.

When you see the stitch dimensions on one of our patterns, you can use exactly this calculation to decide whether you would rather stitch it on 14, 16 or 18 count. The design stays the same; what changes is its scale, texture and the way the project feels in your hands.
